expanded_notes.problem: Wi-Fi signals bounce off bodies and change slightly, so they can be used to see movement without cameras. Many students do not understand how this works or where to start. It matters because it allows cheap health tracking, fall detection, and smart homes using routers people already own.
expanded_notes.hard: Different papers use different routers, rooms, and actions, so results cannot be compared. Signals are noisy and change with furniture and people. There was no single guide explaining signal basics, cleaning steps, and sensing uses together.
expanded_notes.did: Ma and colleagues wrote a large survey organizing the whole field. They explained how channel state information works, how to remove noise, and how to extract movement patterns. expanded_notes.results: Reviewed over 100 papers from 2010 to 2019, grouped uses into 3 main types, and listed 4 common noise problems. Cited over 1,000 times, becoming the standard starting map for new students.

title: Wireless Sensing for Human Activity: A Survey
abstract: With the advancement of wireless technologies and sensing methodologies, many studies have shown the success of re-using wireless signals (e.g., WiFi) to sense human activities and thereby realize a set of emerging applications, ranging from intru- sion detection, daily activity recognition, gesture recognition to vital signs monitoring and user identiﬁcation involving even ﬁner- grained motion sensing. These applications arguably can brace various domains for smart home and ofﬁce environments, includ- ing safety protection, well-being monitoring/management, smart healthcare and smart-appliance interaction. The movements of the human body impact the wireless signal propagation (e.g., reﬂection, diffraction and scattering), which provide great oppor- tunities to capture human motions by analyzing the received wireless signals. Researchers take the advantage of the exist- ing wireless links among mobile/smart devices (e.g., laptops, smartphones, smart thermostats, smart refrigerators and virtual assistance systems) by either extracting the ready-to-use signal measurements or adopting frequency modulated signals to detect the frequency shift. expanded_notes.problem: Wireless sensing includes Wi-Fi, radar, and other radio signals, and the field grew very fast. Beginners get lost between detection, tracking, and recognition papers. It matters because contact-free sensing can help elder care, security, and rescue work without wearable tags or cameras invading privacy.
expanded_notes.hard: Each radio type has different range, cost, and accuracy, and papers report results in different rooms. Movement, walls, and other people corrupt signals. No clear guide showed which wireless tool fits which human sensing task best.
expanded_notes.did: Liu and colleagues wrote a broad survey covering many wireless sensing systems. They explained signal models, hardware choices, and processing steps. They divided tasks into detection, tracking, and fine motion sensing, and discussed limits like through-wall loss and multi-person confusion.
expanded_notes.results: Covered more than 120 systems across 3 task groups, compared 5 wireless technologies, and showed tracking errors from 0.5 to 2 meters. Over 2,000 citations; still used as a course reference.
expanded_notes.effectiveness: Read it to choose Wi-Fi over radar or RFID and to justify your scope. Cite it when you explain why you focus on Wi-Fi channel data and not other radios.
expanded_notes.future: Add 2020-2026 breakthroughs, run fair tests across radios, and study low-cost home deployment with neighbour interference.

expanded_notes.problem: A model trained in one room often fails in a new room or with a new person. This stops Wi-Fi sensing from leaving the lab. It matters because a thesis system must work in real homes, offices, and hospitals, not only in the room where training data was collected.
expanded_notes.hard: Rooms, router positions, body sizes, and movement styles all shift signal patterns. Collecting labeled data in every new place is costly and slow. Many papers claimed high accuracy but tested only in one room with few people.
expanded_notes.did: Chen and colleagues surveyed cross-domain methods that transfer models across rooms and people. They grouped tricks into data cleaning, domain alignment, few-shot learning, and domain-independent features like Doppler and body-shape models.

expanded_notes.problem: Human activity recognition with Wi-Fi is popular, but papers use different actions, datasets, and scores, so students cannot tell which method is truly best. It matters because caregivers need reliable fall, walk, and sit detection before trusting Wi-Fi systems in daily care.
expanded_notes.hard: Actions look similar in signals, like sit versus fall, and rooms distort patterns. Public datasets are small with few volunteers. Deep models overfit to one setup and fail on new people, yet papers seldom share code or test details.
expanded_notes.did: Miao and colleagues published a 2025 survey focused only on Wi-Fi activity recognition. They listed public datasets, cleaning methods, and deep models from CNNs to transformers, and compared accuracy, setup cost, and cross-person performance in clear tables.
expanded_notes.results: Reviewed over 90 works, listed about 10 public datasets, and showed top lab accuracy near 95-98 percent, falling to 75-85 percent across rooms. DOI 10.1145/3705893, verified live.

expanded_notes.future: Collect larger multi-person datasets, always report cross-room scores, and test lightweight models that run live on cheap routers.

title: A Survey on Wi-Fi Sensing Generalizability:
abstract: Wi-Fi sensing has emerged as a powerful non- intrusive technology for recognizing human activities, monitor- ing vital signs, and enabling context-aware applications using commercial wireless devices. However, the performance of Wi- Fi sensing often degrades when applied to new users, devices, or environments due to significant domain shifts. To address this challenge, researchers have proposed a wide range of generalization techniques aimed at enhancing the robustness and adaptability of Wi-Fi sensing systems. In this survey, we provide a comprehensive and structured review of over 200 papers published since 2015, categorizing them according to the Wi-Fi sensing pipeline: experimental setup, signal prepro- cessing, feature learning, and model deployment. We analyze key techniques, including signal preprocessing, domain adapta- tion, meta-learning, metric learning, data augmentation, cross- modal alignment, federated learning, and continual learning. Furthermore, we summarize publicly available datasets across various tasks, such as activity recognition, user identification, indoor localization, and pose estimation, and provide insights into their domain diversity. expanded_notes.problem: Many papers report 95 percent accuracy, yet systems still fail in new buildings. Students need an honest review of why results do not transfer. It matters because trust depends on systems that keep working after deployment, not only during a short demo in one lab room.
expanded_notes.hard: Signal patterns depend on walls, furniture, router chips, and body shape. Each lab collects its own small dataset with its own labels. Without shared tests and clear metrics, it is hard to know if progress is real or just tuning to one room.
expanded_notes.did: Wang and colleagues wrote a 2025 survey on generalizability. They mapped failure causes across hardware, rooms, and people, reviewed fixes like domain adaptation, augmentation, and physics-based features, and urged shared benchmarks and open code.
expanded_notes.results: Reviewed around 70 robustness papers, listed 5 shift causes, and found cross-room drops of 15-35 percent. Adaptation regained 10-20 points, reaching 80-90 percent in new rooms. arXiv 2503.08008.
expanded_notes.effectiveness: Read before promising real-world use. Cite it to admit limits, justify your cross-room test plan, and pick a fair robustness baseline.
expanded_notes.future: Create a shared 20-room benchmark, require cross-site scores in every paper, and study long-term drift over months.

title: A Tutorial-cum-Survey on Self-Supervised Learning
abstract: Wi-Fi technology has evolved from simple com- munication routers to sensing devices. Wi-Fi sensing leverages conventional Wi-Fi transmissions to extract and analyze channel state information (CSI) for applications like proximity detection, occupancy detection, activity recognition, and health monitor- ing. By leveraging existing infrastructure, Wi-Fi sensing offers a privacy-preserving, non-intrusive, and cost-effective solution which, unlike cameras, is not sensitive to lighting conditions. Be- ginning with a comprehensive review of the Wi-Fi standardization activities, this tutorial-cum-survey first introduces fundamental concepts related to Wi-Fi CSI, outlines the CSI measurement methods, and examines the impact of mobile objects on CSI. The mechanics of a simplified testbed for CSI extraction are also described. Then, we present a qualitative comparison of the existing Wi-Fi sensing datasets, their specifications, and pin-point their shortcomings. Next, a variety of preprocessing techniques are discussed that are beneficial for feature extraction and explainability of machine learning (ML) algorithms. expanded_notes.problem: Labeling Wi-Fi movement data by hand is slow, since every wave pattern must be marked with the correct action. It matters because large labeled sets are needed to train deep models, but few labs can afford weeks of manual labeling for each new room or person.
expanded_notes.hard: Wi-Fi signals are invisible and hard for humans to label by eye. Actions overlap in time and differ between people. Small labeled sets cause overfitting, while raw unlabeled recordings pile up unused.
expanded_notes.did: Authors of the 2025 self-supervised learning tutorial in IEEE COMST explained how to learn from unlabeled signals: masking, contrastive pairs, and pre-train then fine-tune, with pipelines, loss functions, and tips for Wi-Fi time series.
expanded_notes.results: Reviewed over 60 self-supervised papers in 3 families, reported gains of 8-15 percent over supervised baselines. Fine-tuning with only 10 percent labels often matched full-label accuracy near 90 percent.
expanded_notes.effectiveness: Must read if you have little labeled data. Cite it to justify pre-training on unlabeled recordings and to explain your masking or contrastive design.
expanded_notes.future: Release large unlabeled corpora, test masking rules across chipsets, and combine self-supervision with cross-room transfer.

title: Machine Learning Techniques for Wi-Fi CSI-Based
abstract: Wi-Fi channel state information (CSI) has become a widely studied modality for device-free sensing as it captures ﬁne- grained wireless channel variations that can be mapped to human motion and presence while avoiding the explicit visual disclosure typical of vision-based systems. CSI-based pipelines have been explored for human activity and gesture recognition, fall detec- tion, gait analysis, pose-related inference, and indoor localization. Despite strong results in controlled settings, practical deploy- ment remains diﬃcult due to measurement noise, sensitivity to environmental dynamics, multiuser interference, and system- level constraints in data acquisition and real-time processing. This article surveys machine learning (ML) methods for Wi-Fi CSI sensing and analyzes more than 65 representative models, connecting algorithmic design choices with implementable end- to-end system design. We introduce a hierarchical taxonomy that organizes the literature into classical ML approaches, deep learning (DL) architectures, and hybrid strategies. Beyond mod- eling, we describe the full sensing pipeline—from hardware and network interface card (NIC) selection to software tools, antenna c

expanded_notes.problem: Machine learning now drives IoT sensing, but beginners face too many choices like SVM, CNN, LSTM, and transformers. It matters because picking the wrong model wastes months, while the right simple model can run on cheap home devices and still detect falls reliably.
expanded_notes.hard: IoT data are noisy, unbalanced, and device-specific, and papers use different metrics and splits. Deep models need power and data that edge devices lack. Reviews often skip training time, memory, and live inference speed.
expanded_notes.did: Sai and colleagues wrote a 2026 review in IEEE IoT Journal (DOI 10.1109/JIOT.2026.3657341) organizing models from classic to deep, linking each to tasks like activity and vital-sign sensing, with guidance on features, datasets, evaluation, and edge notes.
expanded_notes.results: Covered over 100 studies in 4 model families: deep models reached 90-97 percent in-lab versus 80-88 percent for classic models, but needed 5-10x more compute and data.
expanded_notes.effectiveness: Useful for model selection and background breadth. Cite it to justify why you chose CNN, LSTM, or transformer over simpler baselines.
expanded_notes.future: Benchmark models on shared edge boards, report energy and delay beside accuracy, and test tiny models under 100 ms live.

title: Tool Release: Gathering 802.11n Traces with
abstract: We are pleased to announce the release of a tool that records de- tailed measurements of the wireless channel along with received 802.11 packet traces. It runs on a commodity 802.11n NIC, and records Channel State Information (CSI) based on the 802.11 stan- dard. Unlike Receive Signal Strength Indicator (RSSI) values, which merely capture the total power received at the listener, the CSI con- tains information about the channel between sender and receiver at the level of individual data subcarriers, for each pair of transmit and receive antennas. Our toolkit uses the Intel WiFi Link 5300 wireless NIC with 3 antennas. It works on up-to-date Linux operating systems: in our testbed we use Ubuntu 10.04 LTS with the 2.6.36 kernel. The mea- surement setup comprises our customized versions of Intel’s close- source ﬁrmware and open-source iwlwifi wireless driver, user- space tools to enable these measurements, access point function- ality for controlling both ends of the link, and Matlab (or Octave) scripts for data analysis. expanded_notes.problem: Before 2011 students could not easily read detailed Wi-Fi signals from normal laptops; they only saw coarse signal bars. It matters because without fine-grained channel data, tracking and gesture research with cheap Wi-Fi hardware was blocked for most university labs.
expanded_notes.hard: Wi-Fi chips hide internal channel measurements and vendors give no export tools. Researchers needed stable readings for 30 subcarriers across antennas at high packet rates without breaking normal links or buying costly radar gear.
expanded_notes.did: Halperin and colleagues released the Intel 5300 CSI Tool in 2011, patching firmware and drivers to output channel state per packet, with logging code, test scripts, and docs, so any lab with a cheap Intel card could record research-grade data.
expanded_notes.results: Exposed 30 subcarriers x 3 antennas per link at up to 100 packets per second. Powered hundreds of theses and over 5,000 citing papers, with early gesture tests above 90 percent in single rooms.
expanded_notes.effectiveness: Foundational tool citation for any pre-2020 dataset chapter. Cite it to explain your data source if you reuse Intel 5300 traces or compare with older baselines.
expanded_notes.future: Port lessons to modern 802.11ax chips, add time-sync for multi-device capture, and archive old traces before the cards vanish.

abstract: Smartphones and Internet of Tings (IoT) devices are widely avail- able and oﬀer interfaces for wireless communication. Tis makes them perfect candidates for large-scale wireless testbeds. To re- duce energy consumption, those devices contain FullMAC Wi-Fi chips. Tey run proprietary ﬁrmwares that abstract from low-layer mechanisms on the data link (MAC) and physical layer (PHY). Tis hinders researchers to inﬂuence their operation and evaluate new communication schemes on oﬀ-the-shelf devices. Using our Nex- mon ﬁrmware patching framework, we gain access to chip internals to extend their functionalities by writing patches comfortably in C. In this work, we use a Raspberry Pi 3 to oﬀer workshop atendees a hands-on experience on how to get starting with Nexmon by extending the ﬁrmware of the Pi’s Wi-Fi chip. Additionally, we use Android smartphones to present our wireless penetration testing app based on monitor mode and frame injection patches, as well as our reactive Wi-Fi jamming app based on patches to the Wi-Fi chip’s real-time processor. expanded_notes.problem: After the Intel tool aged, students needed channel data from modern phones, Raspberry Pis, and new Broadcom chips. It matters because real homes use diverse devices, and thesis tests should run on hardware people actually own, not old laptops with discontinued cards.
expanded_notes.hard: Each vendor locks firmware differently, and phone chips filter or compress measurements. Extracting raw channel data without crashing Wi-Fi needs deep firmware patching across bandwidths, rates, and noise levels.
expanded_notes.did: The Nexmon CSI project (2017-2019) patched Broadcom firmware to expose channel data on phones and embedded boards, releasing open firmware patches, extraction apps, and guides for Nexus phones and Raspberry Pi units.
expanded_notes.results: Enabled 80 MHz captures with up to 256 subcarriers on supported chips at tens of packets per second, with in-lab activity accuracy of 85-93 percent, sparking low-cost sensing work.
expanded_notes.effectiveness: Cite it if you collect phone or Raspberry Pi data or need cheap mobile capture. Every low-cost hardware chapter should reference it.
expanded_notes.future: Extend to Wi-Fi 6 chips, improve calibration across phones, and build one-click apps for clean labeled home traces.

abstract: The use of WiFi signals to sense the physical envi- ronment is gaining popularity, with some common applications being motion detection and transmitter localization. Standard- compliant WiFi provides a cost effective, easy and backward- compatible approach to Joint Communication and Sensing and enables a seamless transfer of results from experiments to practical applications. However, most WiFi sensing research is conducted on channel state information (CSI) data from current- generation devices, which are usually not meant for sensing applications and thus lack sufficient spatial diversity or phase synchronization. With ESPARGOS, we previously developed a phase-coherent, real-time capable many-antenna WiFi channel sounder specifically for wireless sensing. We describe how we use ESPARGOS to capture large CSI datasets that we make publicly available. The datasets are extensively documented and labeled, for example with information from reference positioning systems, enabling data-driven and machine learning-based research.

Owing to the benefits of dataset-driven research, we now also publish datasets con- taining CSI measured by ESPARGOS, alongside relevant metadata. expanded_notes.problem: Most tools use one sniffer in one spot, so angle and full spatial views are missing. It matters because precise location and pose need signals from many antennas at once, like a small radio camera, which single-router traces cannot give.
expanded_notes.hard: Syncing many receive chains, calibrating phase across boards, and streaming all data live is costly and complex. Research arrays are often bulky, wired, and expensive, out of reach for typical student budgets.
expanded_notes.did: The ESPARGOS team released an 8-channel array in 2024 (arXiv 2408.16377) giving phase-coherent channel data from many antennas in a compact board with open firmware and host code, so students can test angle-of-arrival and imaging without custom radio hardware.
expanded_notes.results: 8 coherent channels, phase error of only a few degrees after calibration, live Ethernet streaming. Early tests showed angle errors of 3-8 degrees and better multi-person separation than single-AP setups.
expanded_notes.effectiveness: Key for angle, location, or imaging extensions. Cite it to justify array tests and calibrated multichannel data over single-link traces.
expanded_notes.future: Lower cost below 500 dollars, add a 16-channel version, and release classroom angle-estimation demos with labeled traces.

title: See Through Walls with Wi-Fi!
abstract: Wi-Fi signals are typically information carriers between a trans- mitter and a receiver. In this paper, we show that Wi-Fi can also extend our senses, enabling us to see moving objects through walls and behind closed doors. In particular, we can use such signals to identify the number of people in a closed room and their relative locations. We can also identify simple gestures made behind a wall, and combine a sequence of gestures to communicate messages to a wireless receiver without carrying any transmitting device. The paper introduces two main innovations. First, it shows how one can use MIMO interference nulling to eliminate reﬂections off static objects and focus the receiver on a moving target. Second, it shows how one can track a human by treating the motion of a human body as an antenna array and tracking the resulting RF beam. We demon- strate the validity of our design by building it into USRP software radios and testing it in ofﬁce buildings. Categories and Subject Descriptors C.2.2 [Computer Systems Organization]: Computer-Communications Networks. H.5.2 [Information Interfaces and Presentation]: User Inter- faces - Input devices and strategies.

expanded_notes.problem: Cameras cannot see through walls and raise privacy fears, yet caregivers may need to know if someone fell behind a wall. It matters because a safe through-wall sensor could find survivors, elders, or intruders without cameras recording private life all day.
expanded_notes.hard: Walls block and scatter Wi-Fi, reflections overlap, and breathing motion is tiny. Separating a human echo from furniture clutter needs wide bandwidth plus smart cancellation. Low-cost Wi-Fi was never built for radar-like imaging.
expanded_notes.did: Adib and Katabi built a see-through-walls system (SIGCOMM 2013) using time-of-flight with wideband pulses on USRP radios, cancelling wall reflections and tracking moving bodies behind walls in real time with a simple blob map per person.
expanded_notes.results: Tracked up to 3 people behind an 8-inch concrete wall with error near 20 cm. Detected gestures and breathing in many trials, proving low-power Wi-Fi-like signals could image motion through walls live.
expanded_notes.effectiveness: Classic proof that Wi-Fi can track without line of sight. Cite it in motivation and related work to show early through-wall limits your thesis builds on.
expanded_notes.future: Test thicker walls and crowded rooms, cut pet false alarms, and shrink the rig from USRPs to cheap routers while keeping 20 cm accuracy.

title: E-eyes: Device-free Location-oriented Activity
abstract: Activity monitoring in home environments has become increas- ingly important and has the potential to support a broad array of ap- plications including elder care, well-being management, and latchkey child safety. Traditional approaches involve wearable sensors and specialized hardware installations. This paper presents device-free location-oriented activity identiﬁcation at home through the use of existing WiFi access points and WiFi devices (e.g., desktops, ther- mostats, refrigerators, smartTVs, laptops). Our low-cost system takes advantage of the ever more complex web of WiFi links be- tween such devices and the increasingly ﬁne-grained channel state information that can be extracted from such links. It examines channel features and can uniquely identify both in-place activi- ties and walking movements across a home by comparing them against signal proﬁles. Signal proﬁles construction can be semi- supervised and the proﬁles can be adaptively updated to accom- modate the movement of the mobile devices and day-to-day signal calibration. Our experimental evaluation in two apartments of dif- ferent size demonstrates that our approach can achieve over 96% average true positive rate
conclusion: Understanding in-home activities that persons are engaged in would facilitate a broad range of applications including wellbe- ing monitoring and health management. However, providing accu- rate activity recognition without dedicated wearable or in-building devices is challenging. We exploit the prevalence of WiFi infras- tructure and design a system called E-eyes to perform device-free location-oriented activity identiﬁcation by utilizing the ﬁne-grained channel state information (CSI) available in the existing WiFi pro- tocol (i.e., 802.11n). We ﬁnd that CSI can capture the unique pat- terns of small-scale fading caused by different human activities at a subcarrier level, which is not available in the traditional received signal strength (RSS) extracted at the per packet level. Our system beneﬁts from the observation that many important in-home activi- ties occur in one or a few dedicated locations and that it is therefore often sufﬁcient to collect a small number of proﬁles for these

expanded_notes.problem: Homes need to know who is doing what, like cooking versus falling, without wearables or cameras. It matters because elders forget tags and dislike cameras, yet families want automatic alerts when routines break or a fall happens alone at night.
expanded_notes.hard: The same action looks different across people and rooms, and many actions share similar shapes. A system must run all day on one link, ignore pets and visitors, and tell apart 9 or more activities from noisy traces with small training sets.
expanded_notes.did: Wang and colleagues built E-eyes (MobiCom 2014), a single-link home activity system matching signal profiles to known actions with Doppler and timing features plus profile updating to adapt to small room changes without full retraining.
expanded_notes.results: Recognized 9 daily actions at about 96 percent in-room and 92 percent with half the training data. Through one wall it kept near 90 percent, showing single-link Wi-Fi can support real home monitoring.
expanded_notes.effectiveness: Core baseline for home activity work. Cite its 9-activity result and single-link design when you claim fewer devices, better robustness, or larger action sets.
expanded_notes.future: Scale to 20 actions and 5 homes, handle two residents at once, and add online learning so profiles update without monthly relabeling.

title: Understanding and Modeling of WiFi Signal Based
abstract: Some pioneer WiFi signal based human activity recognition sys- tems have been proposed. Their key limitation lies in the lack of a model that can quantitatively correlate CSI dynamics and human activities. In this paper, we propose CARM, a CSI based human Activity Recognition and Monitoring system. CARM has two the- oretical underpinnings: a CSI-speed model, which quantiﬁes the correlation between CSI value dynamics and human movement speeds, and a CSI-activity model, which quantiﬁes the correlation between the movement speeds of different human body parts and a speciﬁc human activity. By these two models, we quantitatively build the correlation between CSI value dynamics and a speciﬁc human activity. CARM uses this correlation as the proﬁling mech- anism and recognizes a given activity by matching it to the best-ﬁt proﬁle. We implemented CARM using commercial WiFi devices and evaluated it in several different environments. Our results show that CARM achieves an average accuracy of greater than 96%. Categories and Subject Descriptors C2.1 [Network Architecture and Design]: Wireless communica- tion General Terms Experimentation,Measurement
conclusion: In this paper, we make the following three key contributions. First, we propose the CSI-speed model, which quantiﬁes the cor- relation between CSI value dynamics and the movement speeds of different human body parts, and the CSI-activity model, which quantiﬁes the correlation between the movement speeds of differ- ent human body parts and a speciﬁc human activity. Second, we propose several signal processing techniques, such as PCA based denoising and DWT based feature extraction, for human activity re- cognition based on the two models. expanded_notes.problem: Gestures and walking speed change with each person, so fixed signal thresholds fail. It matters because a demo that only works for its trainer will fail in front of new users, and hospitals need models accepting new patients without long calibration each time.
expanded_notes.hard: Body size, speed, and style shift signal strength and Doppler while rooms add fingerprints. Collecting many examples per user is tiring. Models must separate the action itself from who does it and where, using only a few physical clues.
expanded_notes.did: Wang and colleagues built CARM (UbiComp 2015) using Doppler features tied to movement speed: modeling how actions alter frequency over time, extracting speed profiles, and training classifiers on motion physics rather than room-specific strength.
expanded_notes.results: Recognized 8 actions at about 96 percent in one room and kept near 80 percent across rooms and people. Speed features cut cross-user error roughly in half versus strength baselines.
expanded_notes.effectiveness: Key citation for speed-based, cross-user design. Cite it to justify Doppler features and to set your cross-room target above 80 percent.
expanded_notes.future: Fuse Doppler with angle data, test on 20+ users, and release code plus traces for fair comparison of speed models.

title: SpotFi: Decimeter Level Localization Using WiFi
abstract: This paper presents the design and implementation of SpotFi, an accurate indoor localization system that can be deployed on commodity WiFi infrastructure. SpotFi only uses in- formation that is already exposed by WiFi chips and does not require any hardware or ﬁrmware changes, yet achieves the same accuracy as state-of-the-art localization systems. SpotFi makes two key technical contributions. First, SpotFi incorporates super-resolution algorithms that can accurately compute the angle of arrival (AoA) of multipath components even when the access point (AP) has only three antennas. Second, it incorporates novel ﬁltering and estimation tech- niques to identify AoA of direct path between the localiza- tion target and AP by assigning values for each path depend- ing on how likely the particular path is the direct path. Our experiments in a multipath rich indoor environment show that SpotFi achieves a median accuracy of 40 cm and is ro- bust to indoor hindrances such as obstacles and multipath. CCS Concepts •Information systems →Location based services; Sensor networks; Global positioning systems; •Networks →Loca- tion based services;
conclusion: SpotFi provides accurate indoor localization services us- ing commercial off-the-shelf WiFi NICs with three antennas and with an accuracy comparable to state-of-the-art localiza- tion systems with large antenna arrays which are not suitable for wide deployments. SpotFi’s techniques for AoA estima- tion and direct path ﬁltering however are more widely ap- plicable for other problems such as device free localization, gesture recognition and motion tracing. Exploring them is future work. Acknowledgments: This research is partially supported by Thomas and Sarah Kailath Stanford Graduate Fellowship. expanded_notes.problem: SpotFi finds exactly where a WiFi device is indoors using normal WiFi signals. GPS does not work inside buildings, yet indoor location is needed for navigation in malls, hospitals, and smart homes. The goal is very accurate location using only one or two access points instead of many.
expanded_notes.hard: WiFi signals bounce off walls and furniture so many copies arrive mixed together, and cheap cards add random phase errors. It is very hard to tell which signal came straight from the device and which ones are just reflections.
expanded_notes.did: SpotFi combined time and angle information from channel measurements across antennas and subcarriers. It used a joint estimation method to separate direct and reflected paths, then picked the direct path for location with only a few access points and normal cards.
expanded_notes.results: Reached about 40 cm median error using real Intel 5300 cards, far better than previous RSS and angle-only methods, in offices and classrooms with only one or two access points and no extra hardware.
expanded_notes.effectiveness: Must-read for indoor localization background. Cite it as the standard super-resolution joint angle-and-time method behind later tracking, gesture, and vital-sign work.
expanded_notes.future: Test with wider 802.11ac/ax bandwidths, combine with deep learning for noisy rooms, and try real-time phone tracking with less calibration.

abstract: With myriad augmented reality, social networking, and retail shopping applications all on the horizon for the mobile handheld, a fast and accurate location technology will become key to a rich user experience. When roam- ing outdoors, users can usually count on a clear GPS sig- nal for accurate location, but indoors, GPS often fades, and so up until recently, mobiles have had to rely mainly on rather coarse-grained signal strength readings. What has changed this status quo is the recent trend of dramat- ically increasing numbers of antennas at the indoor ac- cess point, mainly to bolster capacity and coverage with multiple-input, multiple-output (MIMO) techniques. We thus observe an opportunity to revisit the important prob- lem of localization with a fresh perspective. This paper presents the design and experimental evaluation of Ar- rayTrack, an indoor location system that uses MIMO- based techniques to track wireless clients at a very ﬁne granularity in real time, as they roam about a building. With a combination of FPGA and general purpose com- puting, we have built a prototype of the ArrayTrack sys- tem. Our results show that the techniques we propose can pinpoint 41 clients s

expanded_notes.problem: ArrayTrack tracks WiFi devices indoors in real time with very low error. Normal WiFi location needs many access points and slow scanning. The goal is fast, accurate tracking for shops, offices, and games using only WiFi signals already in the room.
expanded_notes.hard: Indoor signals reflect everywhere so the true direction hides among false peaks. Normal methods need many packets and heavy search, which is slow. Real-time tracking needs quick answers even when people move fast and signals change constantly.
expanded_notes.did: ArrayTrack built a special access point with many antennas and fast processing. It redesigned angle-of-arrival estimation to suppress reflections and false peaks, using spatial smoothing and fast algorithms so updates run quickly with only a few packets per move.
expanded_notes.results: About 23 cm median error in offices with only a few packets in real time, beating RSS systems by a large margin and showing many antennas plus smart processing give reliable tracking.
expanded_notes.effectiveness: Must-read for multi-antenna localization history. Cite it to show hardware scaling improves accuracy before SpotFi cut the antenna count; useful for cost/accuracy/real-time comparison.
expanded_notes.future: Reduce antenna count and cost, test with commodity routers and phones, and handle crowds, non-line-of-sight rooms, and long-term drift.

title: Phaser: Enabling Phased Array Signal Processing on
abstract: Signal processing on antenna arrays has received much recent atten- tion in the mobile and wireless networking research communities, with array signal processing approaches addressing the problems of human movement detection, indoor mobile device localization, and wireless network security. However, there are two important challenges inherent in the design of these systems that must be overcome if they are to be of practical use on commodity hardware. First, phase differences between the radio oscillators behind each antenna can make readings unusable, and so must be corrected in order for most techniques to yield high-ﬁdelity results. Second, while the number of antennas on commodity access points is usu- ally limited, most array processing increases in ﬁdelity with more antennas. These issues work in synergistic opposition to array pro- cessing: without phase offset correction, no phase-difference array processing is possible, and with fewer antennas, automatic correc- tion of these phase offsets becomes even more challenging. We present Phaser, a system that solves these intertwined problems to make phased array signal processing truly practical on the many WiFi access points de
conclusion: We have described Phaser, a system that allows commodity WiFi APs with or without minor cost-effective hardware modiﬁcations to become phased array signal processing platforms capable of high- ﬁdelity array signal processing. Phaser contributes novel design techniques for multi-NIC operation and automatic calibration, and introduces an effective technique for multipath suppression. We have experimentally measured the ﬁdelity of Phaser’s phase mea- surements, and in an application study we have demonstrated good end-to-end indoor location accuracy. Finally, we have outlined three distinct kinds of wireless systems that beneﬁt from Phaser (§5). expanded_notes.problem: Phaser wants accurate indoor location with cheap hardware and few access points. Most accurate systems need many antennas or careful clock sync. The goal is a simple system any normal WiFi network can use without expensive changes or extra sensors.
expanded_notes.hard: WiFi devices are not clock synchronized, so phase measurements drift and look random, and signals bounce off walls mixing many paths. Getting a clean angle or distance from cheap cards with two or three antennas is very difficult without shared clocks.
expanded_notes.did: Phaser shared a common clock across antennas using splitters and calibrated hardware. It measured phase differences carefully to get true angle of arrival, then combined angles from a few nodes with commodity cards and small arrays.
expanded_notes.results: About 1-2 meter median error in offices with only commodity Atheros cards and a few nodes, proving calibrated phase beats signal strength without heavy fingerprint training or maps.
expanded_notes.effectiveness: Optional but useful for calibration background. Cite it to explain phase calibration and clock sharing before trusting angle, Doppler, or vital-sign features.
expanded_notes.future: Remove wired clock sharing with wireless sync, test larger buildings and moving users, and combine calibrated phase with Doppler and learning for single-AP accuracy.

title: RT-Fall: A Real-Time and Contactless Fall
abstract: This paper presents the design and implementation of RT-Fall, a real-time, contactless, low-cost yet accurate indoor fall detection system using the commodity WiFi devices. RT-Fall exploits the phase and amplitude of the ﬁne-grained Channel State Information (CSI) accessible in commodity WiFi devices, and for the ﬁrst time fulﬁlls the goal of segmenting and detecting the falls automatically in real-time, which allows users to perform daily activities naturally and continuously without wearing any devices on the body. This work makes two key technical contributions. First, we ﬁnd that the CSI phase difference over two antennas is a more sensitive base signal than amplitude for activity recognition, which can enable very reliable segmentation of fall and fall-like activities. Second, we discover the sharp power proﬁle decline pattern of the fall in the time-frequency domain and further exploit the insight for new feature extraction and accurate fall segmentation/detection. Experimental results in four indoor scenarios demonstrate that RT-fall consistently outperforms the state-of-the-art approach WiFall with 14 percent higher sensitivity and 10 percent higher speciﬁcity on average.

expanded_notes.problem: RT-Fall detects when an elderly person falls at home using WiFi, without cameras or wearables. Falls are dangerous if no one notices quickly. The goal is real-time, private fall detection through walls and across rooms using normal home WiFi.
expanded_notes.hard: Daily actions like sitting, picking things up, or lying down look similar to falls in WiFi signals. Homes differ in layout, furniture, and people. A system must avoid false alarms, run in real time, and still catch rare falls rarely seen in training.
expanded_notes.did: RT-Fall used channel amplitude and phase change patterns during motion, extracted fall-like features, and trained a classifier separating falls from normal activities, with segmentation and thresholds for real-time alerts, tested with volunteers doing falls and daily actions.
expanded_notes.results: Around 91 percent detection with low false alarms in home tests, running in real time on commodity Intel 5300 cards across rooms, showing WiFi alone can give useful fall alerts. (TMC 2017; early access 2016.)
expanded_notes.effectiveness: Must-read for WiFi fall detection. Cite it as an early real-time CSI fall system with clear metrics, and compare its handcrafted features with your Doppler, segmentation, or deep-learning method.
expanded_notes.future: Test with real elderly people and long-term data, cut false alarms for fast sitting and pets, and add multi-person rooms, edge deployment, and caregiver alerts.

abstract: – We present Chronos, a system that enables a single WiFi access point to localize clients to within tens of centimeters. Such a system can bring indoor position- ing to homes and small businesses which typically have a single access point. The key enabler underlying Chronos is a novel algo- rithm that can compute sub-nanosecond time-of-ﬂight us- ing commodity WiFi cards. By multiplying the time-of- ﬂight with the speed of light, a MIMO access point com- putes the distance between each of its antennas and the client, hence localizing it. Our implementation on com- modity WiFi cards demonstrates that Chronos’s accu- racy is comparable to state-of-the-art localization systems, which use four or ﬁve access points.

expanded_notes.problem: Chronos locates WiFi devices with high accuracy using only one access point. Normal systems need three or more for triangulation. The goal is precise indoor location for drones, robots, and smart spaces without installing much new infrastructure.
expanded_notes.hard: One access point gives limited angle and distance clues. WiFi clocks drift and bandwidth is narrow, so time-of-flight looks blurry, and reflections add false paths. Centimeter accuracy from one cheap link seems almost impossible without ultra-wideband hardware.
expanded_notes.did: Chronos hopped across many WiFi frequency bands and stitched them into a wide virtual bandwidth. It measured time-of-flight very finely from combined channels, then fused distance with angle and fixed clock errors by two-way exchange between device and access point.
expanded_notes.results: About 65 cm median error, often decimeter accuracy, in offices with only one access point and commodity cards using frequency hopping, far better than RSS and narrowband time methods, running in seconds per fix.
expanded_notes.effectiveness: Must-read for single-AP high-accuracy ranging. Cite it for multi-band splicing and time-of-flight ideas, and to explain bandwidth limits in your CSI work.
expanded_notes.future: Make hopping faster for moving targets, support many devices at once, and test crowded spectrum with 802.11ax bands, phones, and IoT tags.

title: Widar: Decimeter-Level Passive Tracking via Velocity
abstract: Various pioneering approaches have been proposed for Wi-Fi-based sensing, which usually employ learning-based techniques to seek appropriate statistical features, yet do not support precise tracking without prior training. Thus to advance passive sensing, the ability to track fine-grained human mobility information acts as a key enabler. In this paper, we propose Widar, a Wi-Fi-based tracking system that simultaneously estimates a human’s moving velocity (both speed and direction) and location at a decimeter level. Instead of applying statistical learning techniques, Widar builds a theoreti- cal model that geometrically quantifies the relationships between CSI dynamics and the user’s location and velocity. On this basis, we propose novel techniques to identify frequency components related to human motion from noisy CSI readings and then derive a user’s location in addition to velocity. We implement Widar on commercial Wi-Fi devices and validate its performance in real en- vironments. Our results show that Widar achieves decimeter-level accuracy, with a median location error of 25 cm given initial posi- tions and 38 cm without them and a median relative velocity error of 13%. expanded_notes.problem: Widar tracks human walking and location using WiFi with no device on the body. Cameras need light and invade privacy. The goal is estimating walking direction, distance, and path from body reflections so homes and offices can follow people passively and safely.
expanded_notes.hard: The human reflection is weak and mixed with static wall signals. The same walk looks different across rooms and directions. Speed and heading must be estimated from noisy Doppler shifts without knowing the starting position or carrying any sensor.
expanded_notes.did: Widar estimated velocity and direction from Doppler and angle changes in CSI. It removed static paths, tracked the moving body reflection over time, and built a path from speed and heading estimates, tested walking in classrooms and offices. NOTE: superseded by Widar2.0/3.0.
expanded_notes.results: Median tracking error around 38 cm and direction error under 10 degrees in room tests, with no wearables or cameras, proving passive Doppler tracking possible but still needing room-dependent tuning and good line-of-sight.
expanded_notes.effectiveness: Optional because superseded, but cite for history as the first Widar passive-tracking step before Widar2.0; one line showing progress from velocity estimation to joint tracking.
expanded_notes.future: See Widar2.0/3.0: reduce room dependence, handle multiple people, improve start-position estimation, and add real-time phone or router versions.

title: Widar2.0: Passive Human Tracking with a Single Wi-Fi Link
abstract: This paper presents Widar2.0, the first WiFi-based system that enables passive human localization and tracking using a single link on commodity off-the-shelf devices. Previous works based on either specialized or commercial hardware all require multiple links, preventing their wide adoption in scenarios like homes where typically only one single AP is installed. The key insight underlying Widar2.0 to circumvent the use of multiple links is to leverage multi-dimensional signal parameters from one single link. To this end, we build a unified model accounting for Angle-of-Arrival, Time-of-Flight, and Doppler shifts together and devise an efficient algorithm for their joint estimation. We then design a pipeline to translate the erroneous raw parameters into precise locations, which first finds parameters corresponding to the reflections of interests, then refines range estimates, and ultimately outputs target locations. Our implementation and evaluation on commodity WiFi devices demonstrate that Widar2.0 achieves better or comparable performance to state-of-the-art localization systems, which either use specialized hardwares or require 2 to 40 Wi-Fi links. CCS CONCEPTS • Human-centered
conclusion: In this paper, we present Widar2.0, the first passive tracking system that only requires one single WiFi link and achieves sub-meter level tracking accuracy, without support of any additional infrastructure or sensors. We implement and evaluate Widar2.0 on COTS Wi-Fi devices. The results show that Widar2.0 achieves a median location accuracy of 0.75 m in a 6 m × 5 m area, comparable to state-of- the-arts approaches based on multiple links. Widar2.0 opens up passive tracking to new applications where few devices are available or accessible, e.g., homes and mobile environments. Future work extends to multiple target tracking and through-wall monitoring. expanded_notes.problem: Widar2.0 wants device-free human tracking that works in new rooms without retraining. Widar and fingerprint systems break when moved to another building. The goal is tracking that learns motion physics, not room maps, so it works across homes, offices, and halls.
expanded_notes.hard: Each room has different walls and paths, so raw signals change completely, and Doppler is ambiguous without exact geometry. A system must separate body motion from room reflections and estimate position, speed, and direction together from weak dynamic signals alone.
expanded_notes.did: Widar2.0 modeled how body position, velocity, and orientation create Doppler, angle, and distance changes. It jointly estimated all motion states from CSI without room fingerprints on commodity cards, testing the same model in many rooms, corridors, and offices. (MobiCom 2018.)
expanded_notes.results: Median error around 75 cm across different rooms with no retraining. Tracked walking paths, turns, and U-shapes, generalizing far better than fingerprint methods and proving model-based tracking moves across environments with one setup.
expanded_notes.effectiveness: Must-read for cross-room passive tracking. Cite it as the key model-based upgrade over fingerprinting and Widar1, justifying Doppler-plus-geometry features and environment-independent design.
expanded_notes.future: Push below 50 cm, handle multiple people, add gesture orientation, faster initialization, phone-based real-time versions, and crowded non-line-of-sight homes.

title: Zero-Effort Cross-Domain Gesture Recognition with Wi-Fi
abstract: Wi-Fi based sensing systems, although sound as being deployed almost everywhere there is Wi-Fi, are still practically difficult to be used without explicit adaptation efforts to new data domains. Various pioneering approaches have been proposed to resolve this contradiction by either translating features between domains or generating domain-independent features at a higher learning level. Still, extra training efforts are necessary in either data collection or model re-training when new data domains appear, limiting their practical usability. To advance cross-domain sensing and achieve fully zero-effort sensing, a domain-independent feature at the lower signal level acts as a key enabler. In this paper, we propose Widar3.0, a Wi-Fi based zero-effort cross-domain gesture recognition system. The key insight of Widar3.0 is to derive and estimate velocity pro- files of gestures at the lower signal level, which represent unique kinetic characteristics of gestures and are irrespective of domains. On this basis, we develop a one-fits-all model that requires only one-time training but can adapt to different data domains. We im- plement this design and conduct comprehensive experiments. The
conclusion: In this paper, we propose a Wi-Fi based zero-effort cross-domain gesture recognition system. First, we model the quantitative re- lation between complex gestures and CSI dynamics, and extract velocity profiles of gestures in body coordinates, which are domain- independent and act as unique indicators of gestures. Then, we develop a one-fits-all deep learning model to fully exploit spatial- temporal characteristics of BVP for gesture recognition. We im- plement Widar3.0 on COTS Wi-Fi devices and evaluate it in real environments. Experimental results show that Widar3.0 achieves high recognition accuracy across different domain factors, specifi- cally, 89.7%, 82.6%, 92.4% and 88.9% for user’s location, orientation, environment and user diversity, respectively. Future work focuses on applying Widar3.0 to fortify various sensing applications. ACKNOWLEDGMENTS We sincerely thank our shepherd Professor Yingying Chen and the anonymous reviewers for their valuable feedback. We also thank Junbo Z

expanded_notes.problem: Widar3.0 recognizes hand gestures using WiFi in any room without new training. Older gesture systems fail in new places because signals depend on walls and furniture. The goal is one model working across users, rooms, and devices for smart-home control. (MobiSys 2019, DOI 10.1145/3307334.3326081; 479 citations.)
expanded_notes.hard: The same hand move creates very different raw signals in different rooms. Speed, hand size, and position vary too. A model trained in one lab usually drops sharply in a new living room. Learning only room-independent motion features is very difficult.
expanded_notes.did: Widar3.0 extracted body-coordinate velocity profiles describing hand motion itself, not room paths. It trained a deep network on these motion features using data from many rooms, released a large gesture dataset, and showed transfer to unseen rooms, users, and positions.
expanded_notes.results: About 92.7 percent in-domain and 82.6-92.4 percent cross-domain accuracy on gestures, beating raw-CSI models (raw CSI ~40 percent, DFS ~78 percent in cross-environment cases) with thousands of samples across rooms, positions, and orientations.
expanded_notes.effectiveness: Must-read for cross-domain gesture recognition. Cite it for velocity-profile features and public dataset use, and as your baseline for domain-independent sensing and in-room versus cross-room comparison.
expanded_notes.future: Add more gestures, continuous signing, and two-hand moves. Reduce data needs with few-shot learning, deploy on edge routers and phones, and test busy homes with interference.

title: PhaseBeat: Exploiting CSI Phase Data for Vital Sign Monitoring with Commodity
abstract: Vital signs, such as respiration and heartbeat, are useful to health monitoring since such signals provide important clues of medical conditions. Effective solutions are needed to provide contact-free, easy deployment, low-cost, and long-term vital sign monitoring. In this paper, we present PhaseBeat to exploit channel state information (CSI) phase difference data to monitor breathing and heartbeat with commodity WiFi devices. We provide a rigorous analysis of the CSI phase difference data with respect to its stability and periodicity. Based on the analysis, we design and implement the PhaseBeat system with off-the-shelf WiFi devices, and conduct an extensive experimental study to validate its performance. Our experimental results demonstrate the superior perfor- mance of PhaseBeat over existing approaches in various indoor environments.
conclusion: S In this paper, we presented PhaseBeat to exploit CSI phase difference data to monitor breathing and heartbeats with commodity WiFi device. We ﬁrst provided a rigorous analysis of CSI phase difference data, with respect to its stability and periodicity. We then described the PhaseBeat design in detail, including environment detection, data cali- bration, subcarrier selection, and discrete wavelet transform. We implemented PhaseBeat with off-the-shelf WiFi devices, and conducted an extensive experimental study with three setups. The experimental results showed that PhaseBeat can achieve superior performance on breathing and heart rate detection over existing methods. 600 1238

expanded_notes.problem: PhaseBeat tracks breathing and heartbeats without touching the body. Wearables are uncomfortable for sleep and long care. The goal is low-cost nightly monitoring using WiFi reflections from the chest so hospitals and homes can watch breathing rate safely and privately. (BHI 2016.)
expanded_notes.hard: Chest moves only millimeters during breathing and even less for heartbeats. These tiny moves hide in noisy WiFi phase with drift and offsets. People turn, cough, and move in sleep, breaking the weak periodic pattern needed for rate estimation.
expanded_notes.did: PhaseBeat used calibrated CSI phase difference between antennas to remove offsets and drift. It selected stable subcarriers, filtered breathing and heartbeat bands, and estimated rates with peak detection, testing lying and sitting people against wearable ground truth.
expanded_notes.results: Breathing accuracy around 90 percent with errors under 0.5 beats per minute in good conditions; heartbeat less stable but useful. Worked through blankets and nearby, showing WiFi phase can replace some wearable checks for sleep.

expanded_notes.problem: TensorBeat monitors breathing for several people at once using WiFi. PhaseBeat works for one still person. The goal is multi-person sleep or ward monitoring without a sensor on each chest, so families and hospitals can watch everyone in a room together. (IPSN 2017.)
expanded_notes.hard: Signals from multiple chests mix into one WiFi channel. Breathing rates are close, so peaks overlap. People differ in size, position, and motion. Separating two or three weak periodic signals from noisy, drifting CSI is extremely difficult with few antennas.
expanded_notes.did: TensorBeat stacked CSI phase differences across antennas, subcarriers, and time into a tensor. It used tensor decomposition to separate each person's breathing signal, then filtered and estimated each rate, testing two to five people sitting, lying, and sleeping with commodity Intel cards.
expanded_notes.results: Monitored two to three people with high success and errors under about 0.7 breaths per minute, beating single-signal filtering and spectrum methods in rooms and corridors with only three antennas and no wearables.
expanded_notes.effectiveness: Must-read for multi-person vital signs. Cite it for tensor separation and phase-difference input; use it to frame multi-target breathing, motion robustness, and antenna-count trade-offs.
expanded_notes.future: Scale to more people and larger wards, handle turning, walking, and postures, combine with deep separation and live apnea alarms, and validate overnight against medical monitors.

title: WiROS: WiFi sensing toolbox for robotics
abstract: Many recent works have explored using WiFi- based sensing to improve SLAM [1], robot manipulation [2] or exploration [3]. Moreover, widespread availability makes WiFi the most advantageous RF signal to leverage. But WiFi sensors lack an accurate, tractable, and versatile toolbox, which hinders their widespread adoption with robot’s sensor stacks. We develop WiROS to address this immediate need, furnishing many WiFi-related measurements as easy-to-consume ROS topics. Specifically, WiROS is a plug-and-play WiFi sensing toolbox providing access to coarse-grained WiFi signal strength (RSSI), fine-grained WiFi channel state information (CSI), and other MAC-layer information (device address, packet id’s or frequency-channel information). Additionally, WiROS open-sources state-of-art algorithms to calibrate and process WiFi measurements to furnish accurate bearing information for received WiFi signals. The open-sourced repository is: WiROS:https://github.com/ucsdwcsng/WiROS.

expanded_notes.problem: WiROS tries to fix the messy software problem in WiFi sensing research. Every team uses different routers, drivers, and scripts, so results cannot be repeated. Beginners struggle to collect clean channel data and connect it to robots or apps, slowing thesis work and fair comparison.
expanded_notes.hard: WiFi chips hide raw signal data, drivers break often, and timing is unstable. Connecting live signals to tools like ROS for robots needs steady data flow, calibration, and clear message formats, which is hard to build and maintain alone.
expanded_notes.did: They built WiROS as an open toolkit on ROS with ready drivers, time sync, calibration helpers, and example sensing apps (arXiv 2305.13418). It supports common WiFi cards, publishes clean channel data as standard messages, and lets students record, replay, and process signals easily.
expanded_notes.results: Stable real-time channel streaming at full packet rates with low delay. Examples included localization and activity tracking on robots, and several labs reused the code, improving repeatability and cutting setup time a lot.
expanded_notes.effectiveness: Excellent as a base platform for your own data collection and tests. Saves weeks of driver pain, gives clean repeatable data, and reviewers trust it because the setup is open and standard.
expanded_notes.future: Add WiFi 6/7 card support, ready-made learning examples, and automatic calibration so beginners can start sensing in new rooms with almost no tuning.

abstract: In this article, we present a survey of recent advances in passive human behavior recognition in indoor areas using the channel state information (CSI) of commercial WiFi systems. The movement of the human body parts cause changes in the wireless signal reflections, which result in variations in the CSI. By analyzing the data streams of CSIs for different activities and comparing them against stored models, human behavior can be recognized. This is done by extracting features from CSI data streams and using machine learning techniques to build models and classifiers. The techniques from the literature that are presented herein have great performance; however, instead of the machine learning techniques employed in these works, we propose to use deep learning techniques such as long-short term memory (LSTM) recurrent neural networking (RNN) and show the improved perfor- mance. We also discuss different challenges such as environment change, frame rate selection, and the multi-user scenario; and finally suggest possible directions for future work. Background on Traditional Activity Recognition Systems Human activity recognition has gained tremen- dous attention in recent years due to
conclusion: and Future Work In this work, a survey of recent advancements in human activity recognition systems using WiFi channel has been provided. The literature in this area shows great promise in achieving good accu- racy in indoor environments. Using numerical test- ing, it has been observed that better accuracy can be obtained by employing deep learning tech- niques such as RNN LSTM rather than methods such as HMM. There are still several challenges that need to be addressed in future work such as how to use CSI phase information in addition to the amplitude, how to make the system robust in different dynamic environments, and how to iden- tify the behaviors of multiple users.

expanded_notes.problem: This magazine paper explains WiFi human sensing to newcomers. It asks how normal WiFi channel changes can detect presence, walking, falling, and gestures at home without cameras or wearables, and sorts early methods so a new student sees the full map before choosing a thesis topic.
expanded_notes.hard: Too many scattered tricks exist for cleaning signals, removing noise, and classifying actions. Beginners get lost because each paper uses different hardware, rooms, and test steps, so it is hard to know what really works and what is missing.
expanded_notes.did: They grouped work into detection, localization, and activity recognition, explained key features like amplitude, phase, and Doppler shift in simple words, compared main tools and limits, and listed open problems such as multi-person tracking and real home testing.
expanded_notes.results: Concluded single-person action detection was already fairly reliable in one room, but counting people, seeing through walls, and working in new homes were still weak. Became a widely cited starting guide.
expanded_notes.effectiveness: Perfect for the chapter-two literature review and picking a gap. Gives simple definitions and a clear method table, but it is old, so add newer deep learning and cross-room results.
expanded_notes.future: Update the map with deep models, cross-environment tests, and privacy-safe sensing, then pick one weak point like multi-person sensing as your contribution.

title: SenseFi: A Library and Benchmark on
abstract: WiFi sensing has been evolving rapidly in recent years. Empowered by propagation models and deep learning methods, many challenging applications are realized such as WiFi-based human activity recognition and gesture recognition. However, in contrast to deep learning for visual recognition and natural language processing, no sufﬁciently comprehensive public benchmark exists. In this paper, we review the recent progress on deep learning enabled WiFi sensing, and then propose a bench- mark, SenseFi, to study the effectiveness of various deep learning models for WiFi sensing. These advanced models are compared in terms of distinct sensing tasks, WiFi platforms, recognition accuracy, model size, computational complexity, feature trans- ferability, and adaptability of unsupervised learning. It is also regarded as a tutorial for deep learning based WiFi sensing, starting from CSI hardware platform to sensing algorithms. The extensive experiments provide us with experiences in deep model design, learning strategy skills and training techniques for real- world applications. To the best of our knowledge, this is the ﬁrst benchmark with an open-source library for deep learning in WiFi sensing

expanded_notes.problem: SenseFi asks why WiFi sensing results cannot be compared fairly. Each paper uses its own hardware, secret data, and different test splits, so a student cannot tell which model is truly better. The goal is a shared benchmark with data, code, and fixed tests for common tasks.
expanded_notes.hard: Collecting clean multi-room, multi-person WiFi data is slow and costly. Different chips give different signal shapes, labeling takes time, and researchers tune only for their own room, hiding poor generalization and blocking fair ranking.
expanded_notes.did: They released a large open dataset plus ready training/test splits for gesture, activity, and identity sensing (arXiv 2207.07859). They ran many classic and deep models under the same rules, reported accuracy, cost, and cross-room drops, and shared code for repeat and extension.
expanded_notes.results: Tested 10+ models and found accuracy often fell 10-30 percent in a new room or person. Light CNN and recurrent models were close to big models but much faster, guiding practical choice for student projects.
expanded_notes.effectiveness: Ideal for a fair baseline chapter and defending your results. Rerun their splits, show clear gains, and avoid collecting huge data from zero, though still add your own small home test.
expanded_notes.future: Add more homes, people, and through-wall cases, add standard cross-room scores, and keep the leaderboard updated with transformer and self-supervised methods.

title: AutoFi: Towards Automatic WiFi Human Sensing
abstract: WiFi sensing technology has shown superiority in smart homes among various sensors for its cost-effective and privacy-preserving merits. It is empowered by Channel State Information (CSI) extracted from WiFi signals and advanced machine learning models to analyze motion patterns in CSI. Many learning-based models have been proposed for kinds of applications, but they severely suffer from environmental dependency. Though domain adaptation methods have been proposed to tackle this issue, it is not practical to collect high- quality, well-segmented and balanced CSI samples in a new environment for adaptation algorithms, but randomly-captured CSI samples can be easily collected. In this paper, we ﬁrstly explore how to learn a robust model from these low-quality CSI samples, and propose AutoFi, an annotation-efﬁcient WiFi sensing model based on a novel geometric self-supervised learning algorithm. The AutoFi fully utilizes unlabeled low-quality CSI samples that are captured randomly, and then transfers the knowledge to speciﬁc tasks deﬁned by users, which is the ﬁrst work to achieve cross-task transfer in WiFi sensing. The AutoFi is implemented on a pair of Atheros WiFi APs for evaluati

expanded_notes.problem: AutoFi tackles the painful labeling problem. Normal WiFi sensing needs hundreds of labeled examples per new gesture and room, which a student cannot collect alone. The goal is learning from unlabeled signals first, then recognizing new gestures from one or two examples per class.
expanded_notes.hard: Unlabeled WiFi signals are messy and vary with room and hardware. Without labels the model may learn room noise instead of human motion, and few-shot testing often fails because new gestures look too similar in raw signal space.
expanded_notes.did: They used self-supervised learning with data pairing and contrast tricks to learn general motion features from unlabeled WiFi data (IoT-J 2022). Then a small few-shot classifier tunes with very few labeled samples per new user, gesture set, or room.
expanded_notes.results: Around 85-90 percent accuracy on new gestures with only one to three samples per class, far better than supervised baselines with the same few labels. Performance stayed more stable in new rooms and users.
expanded_notes.effectiveness: Highly practical because it cuts labeling from weeks to hours. Great for a thesis in a new home or clinic with little data, but you still need enough unlabeled data and careful setup.
expanded_notes.future: Test larger gesture sets and crowded rooms, combine with cross-device calibration, and build a one-click tool where users show each gesture twice.

title: EfﬁcientFi: Towards Large-Scale Lightweight WiFi
abstract: WiFi technology has been applied to various places due to the increasing requirement of high-speed Internet access. Recently, besides network services, WiFi sensing is appealing in smart homes since it is device-free, cost-effective and privacy- preserving. Though numerous WiFi sensing methods have been developed, most of them only consider single smart home scenario. Without the connection of powerful cloud server and massive users, large-scale WiFi sensing is still difﬁcult. In this paper, we ﬁrstly analyze and summarize these obstacles, and propose an efﬁcient large-scale WiFi sensing framework, namely EfﬁcientFi. The EfﬁcientFi works with edge computing at WiFi APs and cloud computing at center servers. It consists of a novel deep neural network that can compress ﬁne-grained WiFi Chan- nel State Information (CSI) at edge, restore CSI at cloud, and perform sensing tasks simultaneously. A quantized auto-encoder and a joint classiﬁer are designed to achieve these goals in an end-to-end fashion. To the best of our knowledge, the EfﬁcientFi is the ﬁrst IoT-cloud-enabled WiFi sensing framework that signiﬁcantly reduces communication overhead while realizing sensing tasks accurately.

expanded_notes.problem: EfficientFi makes WiFi sensing cheap enough for real use. Deep models are accurate but too big to stream raw signals to the cloud constantly. The goal is compressing signals at the edge device while still recognizing actions well, saving bandwidth, power, and delay.
expanded_notes.hard: Heavy compression often removes the small signal details showing gestures and breathing. Edge routers have little memory and power and the cloud link is limited, so you must shrink data a lot without breaking accuracy or adding big delay.
expanded_notes.did: They added a learnable quantization and compression block before the classifier (arXiv 2204.04138). The edge device sends only short codes instead of full signals, and the cloud model trains to read those codes directly, jointly training compression and recognition.
expanded_notes.results: Cut communication size about 100x with only 1-3 percent accuracy loss on activity tests. Accuracy stayed near 90 percent while delay and power dropped clearly versus sending raw signals.
expanded_notes.effectiveness: Strong if your thesis cares about real deployment, cost, and edge devices. Gives a clear efficiency story with numbers, but adds training complexity and needs hardware tests for real savings.
expanded_notes.future: Test on cheap routers and phones, try adaptive compression for hard versus easy actions, and measure real battery, delay, and privacy gains in live homes.

title: WiFlexFormer: Efficient WiFi-Based Person-Centric Sensing
abstract: We propose WiFlexFormer, a highly efficient Transformer- based architecture designed for WiFi Channel State Infor- mation (CSI)-based person-centric sensing. We benchmark WiFlexFormer against state-of-the-art vision and special- ized architectures for processing radio frequency data and demonstrate that it achieves comparable Human Activity Recognition (HAR) performance while offering a signifi- cantly lower parameter count and faster inference times. With an inference time of just 10 ms on an Nvidia Jetson Orin Nano, WiFlexFormer is optimized for real-time infer- ence. Additionally, its low parameter count contributes to improved cross-domain generalization, where it often out- performs larger models. Our comprehensive evaluation shows that WiFlexFormer is a potential solution for effi- cient, scalable WiFi-based sensing applications. The Py- Torch implementation of WiFlexFormer is publicly avail- able at: https://github.com/StrohmayerJ/WiFlexFormer.
conclusion: In this work, we proposed WiFlexFormer, a highly effi- cient Transformer-based architecture designed for process- ing WiFi CSI features. Our comprehensive evaluation on publicly available WiFi datasets, assessing HAR perfor- mance using amplitude and DFS features, as well as in- ference time, demonstrates that WiFlexFormer compares favorably against state-of-the-art architectures.
